title: Evaluating Protective Role of MSC-Derived Exosomes Against E-Cigarette-Induced Submandibular Salivary Gland Injury in Adult Male Albino Rats: Biochemical, Histological, and Immunohistochemical Evidence
content: Background: E-cigarettes are increasingly taken up as a substitute for conventional smoking. However, the production of e-cigarette smoke can have adverse effects on the body, including inflammation and the induction of oxidative stress and damage to multiple organ systems, including the salivary glands. Exosomes secreted by mesenchymal stem cells, exhibit regenerative and antioxidant properties. However, the potential protective effects of MSC-Exos on the salivary glands from the adverse effects of e-cigarettes has yet to be explored. Aim: Evaluate the ability of MSC-derived exosomes to mitigate submandibular salivary gland injury resulting from e-cigarette exposure in adult male rats. Also, evaluate the contribution of oxidative stress and inflammation, focusing on the Nrf2/NF-κB/NLRP3 signaling pathways. Materials and Methods: In total, 40 adult male albino rats were randomly divided into 4 groups, Control, MSC-Exosome, E-Cigarette, and combined E-Cigarette and MSC-Exosome (n=10 per group). MSC-Exosomes were administered through tail vein injections at 100 µg protein equivalent, administered 2 times per week for 8 weeks. Rats in the E-Cigarette group were exposed to whole body aerosol of e-liquid (1 mL/day, 18 mg/mL nicotine) 5 days a week for 8 weeks. Glands were prepared for Histology and stained with H &amp; E and Masson's trichrome with immunochemistry for both Nrf2 and NF-κB. SOD, CAT, GSH and MDA, in addition to the inflammatory markers NLRP3 and caspase-1 were obtained as results of oxidative stress. Results: For the e-cigarette group, the glands demonstrated notable degeneration alongside several inflammatory changes, while collagen deposition increased. Additionally, MDA levels increased and antioxidant defenses (diminished SOD, CAT, and GSH) were lessened. NF-κB, NLRP3, and caspase-1 expressions were increased and Nrf2 immunoreactivity decreased. The administration of MSC-Exosomes helped restore glandular structure and improved antioxidant defenses. Fibrosis, along with alterations of inflammatory signaling, were also lessened. Conclusion: Exosomes derived from mesenchymal stem cells offered clear protection against salivary injury from e-cigarette exposure. By engaging the Nrf2 antioxidant pathway and inhibiting inflammatory cascades mediated by NF-κB/NLRP3/caspase-1, exosomes offered significant protection against submandibular salivary gland damage from e-cigarettes. Collectively, these findings distinguish these exosomes as a unique and highly novel, cell-free therapeutic application, derived from living stem cells, that addresses salivary gland injury from vaping
